name: persuasion_v3
instructions: You are annotating a charity-donation chat in which a persuader tries to get the persuadee to donate to Save the Children. Tag ONLY the final message, given after 'Persuader message to tag:' (earlier turns are context to interpret it). Choose the persuasion strategy or dialogue act the final message performs. Decide by what the message does in context, not by topic.

criteria.greeting: Hello/hi/good morning, 'how are you' pleasantries and replies to them ('I am well', 'Doing ok here'), and small talk about one's day or the weather ('Pretty good, sitting at my desk enjoying the weather'), goodbyes.
criteria.acknowledgement: ONLY a very short standalone agreement, echo or reaction to what the other person just said: 'I agree.', 'Yes, I think so too', 'Great!', 'Me too!', 'That is amazing!', 'Okay', 'Yes it is'. If the message is longer, adds an opinion, a reason or a new idea ('That's a good idea actually, that way you know your efforts help', 'We could all do better, I suppose'), it is NOT acknowledgement: use other (or the matching strategy).
criteria.thank: The persuader thanks the persuadee (for their time, their donation, their answer). 'Thank you so much for your donation!' 'Thanks for chatting.' Also a follow-up to a thank-you such as 'The children will appreciate it.' NOT 'you're welcome' and NOT confirming a donation amount.
criteria.praise-user: Complimenting the persuadee as a person: 'you are very generous', 'I see I got a really kind person', 'That is very generous of you', 'you are a wonderful person'.
criteria.ask-donation-amount: A QUESTION asking how much/what amount/what percentage they will give, or offering a choice of amounts: 'How much would you like to give?', 'What is a typical donation?', 'Could you afford fifteen cents?', 'Say $500?'. A statement that merely suggests or names an amount ('we usually suggest a monthly donation of $5') is proposition-of-donation.
criteria.proposition-of-donation: Invites or asks the persuadee to donate, or to take the opportunity to help: 'Would you like to donate?', 'Would you be willing to donate some of your payment?', 'You can donate now', 'My job today is to see if you would donate your earnings', 'What if I told you that you have the opportunity to change the world? Would you take it?', and suggestions of a specific amount as a proposal ('we suggest $5 a month', 'I was thinking a dollar to start').
criteria.foot-in-the-door: RARE class. Only an explicit minimising move: 'It only takes pocket change', 'just a few cents', 'even a penny helps', 'every little bit counts', aimed at making the request feel trivial. NOT statements that a small sum buys a concrete result ('$1 feeds a child for a day', 'a week's worth of coffee helps a child for weeks') - those are logical-appeal - and NOT statements about children's suffering (emotion-appeal).
criteria.donation-information: Practical facts about how donating works: amount range ($0 to all your payment), deducted from task payment, research team collects it, website/URL, payment methods, where/how to donate, the task procedure.
criteria.credibility-appeal: Establishes the charity's (or persuader's) credibility: what the organization is and does in general terms ('Save the Children is an international NGO that promotes children's rights'), its history, size, ratings, efficiency ('only 5% to administration'), partners, endorsements, transparency.
criteria.logical-appeal: Reasoning about why donating is effective or sensible: a small amount produces a concrete effect ('30 cents can feed a child'), money goes where needed, everyone can afford it, donation matching, rational arguments about impact or cost, reasons why the cause matters for people or society ('this is important for my family and everybody who needs help').
criteria.emotion-appeal: Evokes sympathy, guilt, sadness or hope using emotional language or vivid suffering of children: 'It's heartbreaking that kids lack clean water', casualty statistics of children killed or injured, 'the children are our future', 'think of the children', the persuader's own feelings of being troubled or moved, reports of what donations achieved for children ('1000 children were saved from hunger'), 'Save the Children does whatever it takes to ensure children grow up healthy'.
criteria.personal-story: An anecdote or narrative about the persuader's own life/feelings or about a specific child: 'Bruce was born to a single mother...', 'I have a fridge full of food and a roof over my head'.
criteria.self-modeling: The persuader says that they themselves donate, volunteer or will donate, to set an example: 'I donate monthly', 'I'll donate 70% and you do 30%', 'I do!' (answering whether they donate). Not merely using 'we' or 'supporters like me and you' in a generic appeal (that is emotion-appeal).
criteria.source-related-inquiry: Asks the persuadee whether they have heard of or know the charity Save the Children itself: 'Have you heard of Save the Children?', 'What do you know about this organization?'.
criteria.task-related-inquiry: Asks the persuadee's opinion, expectations or feelings about donating or the task: 'What do you think?', 'Does this sound like a good charity?', 'How do you feel about donating?'. Not amount questions. If the message says the survey/charity is a good cause and then asks 'Do you agree?', it is credibility-appeal.
criteria.personal-related-inquiry: Asks about the persuadee personally: donation history, volunteering, family/children, where they live, what they do, 'Do you donate to charities?', 'Do you have children?'.
criteria.off-task: RARE class. Only clearly unrelated topics with no link to the charity or the chat task, e.g. geography trivia or opinions on politics/history unrelated to donating. NOT small talk about one's day or the weather (that is greeting), NOT comments about the chat procedure ('we need 10 chats to finish') (other).
criteria.other: Anything else: clarifying or interest-check questions ('What are you not sure about?', 'Would you be interested in that?', 'Do you want some info?'), comments about the chat procedure ('we need 10 chats each to complete this hit'), typo corrections ('Sorry, typo!'), remarks that merely comment or muse without persuading ('We could all do better, I suppose', 'Actually, I'm really troubled by the answer' in reply to a rebuff), 'you're welcome', confirming or closing a donation amount ('To confirm, you said 20 cents, correct?'), filler.
